blocks.content: The acknowledgments topic ended with a forward pointer: several duplicate acknowledgments in a row are a meaningful signal that something is genuinely missing. This topic delivers the full mechanics, exactly how and when TCP decides to resend lost data, closing out the mechanical trio of sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and this topic.

TCP never gets a direct notification that says, this specific piece of data was lost. It has to INFER loss from indirect signals. This topic covers the two real mechanisms TCP actually uses to make that inference.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437538590-600378038.png
1. Mechanism One: Timeout Based Retransmission

Every time the sender sends data, it starts a timer. If the expected acknowledgment for that data does not arrive before the timer expires, the sender assumes the data was lost somewhere and resends it. Simple and reliable as a fallback, but the real downside has to be stated honestly, waiting for a timeout takes real time, since the timer has to be set conservatively enough to avoid false alarms on a merely slow but not actually lost segment.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437538590-716297634.png
2. How the Timeout Duration Is Actually Chosen
blocks.text: 2. How the Timeout Duration Is Actually Chosen

blocks.content: TCP does not use one single fixed timeout value for every connection. It continuously measures the actual round trip time on that specific connection and adapts its timeout based on real observed conditions. A connection with a naturally slow, high latency path gets a longer timeout than a fast, low latency one, avoiding constant false alarms on paths that are simply inherently slower.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437538591-101344134.png
blocks.alt: How the Timeout Duration Is Actually Chosen

blocks.content: 3. Mechanism Two: Fast Retransmission via Duplicate Acknowledgments
blocks.text: 3. Mechanism Two: Fast Retransmission via Duplicate Acknowledgments

blocks.content: Picking up directly from the acknowledgments topic, if the sender receives several duplicate acknowledgments in a row, the same acknowledgment number repeated multiple times, this is a strong, immediate signal that a specific piece of data is genuinely missing. Rather than waiting for the potentially slow timeout to eventually expire, TCP treats a small number of duplicate acknowledgments, in practice three, as a trigger to immediately resend the missing data right away, dramatically faster than waiting for a timeout.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437538591-749379166.png
blocks.alt: Mechanism Two: Fast Retransmission via Duplicate Acknowledgments

blocks.title: Why three specifically
blocks.content: A single duplicate acknowledgment can just mean a segment briefly arrived out of order and will sort itself out. Requiring a small number in a row, rather than acting on just one, filters out this harmless case while still reacting quickly to genuine loss.
4. A Full Worked Example of Fast Retransmission
blocks.text: 4. A Full Worked Example of Fast Retransmission

blocks.content: Bytes 1000 to 1499 are lost, but bytes 1500 to 1999, 2000 to 2499, and 2500 to 2999 all arrive successfully afterward. Since the receiver cannot acknowledge past the gap, tying back to cumulative acknowledgment from the acknowledgments topic, it sends the same acknowledgment number, still asking for byte 1000, three separate times in response to each of those later arriving segments. The sender sees these three duplicate acknowledgments and immediately resends bytes 1000 to 1499 without waiting for any timeout at all.

blocks.alt: A Full Worked Example of Fast Retransmission

6. The One Case Only Timeout Can Catch
blocks.text: 6. The One Case Only Timeout Can Catch

blocks.content: If the lost segment is the very LAST one sent with nothing after it, there is nothing to trigger duplicate acknowledgments at all. Timeout is the only mechanism that can catch that specific case.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437538592-834069253.png
blocks.alt: The One Case Only Timeout Can Catch

blocks.content: 7. Why Having Both Mechanisms Together Matters
blocks.text: 7. Why Having Both Mechanisms Together Matters

blocks.content: Fast retransmission handles the common case quickly when enough surrounding data exists to trigger it. Timeout based retransmission is the reliable, guaranteed fallback that catches everything else, including the case where fast retransmission genuinely cannot apply. Together they give TCP both speed in the common case and a hard guarantee in every case.

Waiting for a reply text that never comes captures this well. Either you eventually give up and resend it yourself after enough time passes, timeout, or a friend who received your later messages mentions never getting an earlier one, prompting you to immediately resend that specific message right away, without waiting, fast retransmission.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437538592-123483432.png
blocks.alt: Why Having Both Mechanisms Together Matters

blocks.content: 8. The Real Cost of Retransmission

Retransmitting is not free, it adds extra traffic onto a network that may already be under some degree of stress. A lost segment being interpreted as a sign of congestion is exactly the connection point back to the congestion control topic reaction to detected loss, tying this whole reliability machinery directly back to that earlier topic.

blocks.title: Loss means two things happen at once
blocks.content: A lost segment triggers both a retransmission here, to recover the missing data, and a congestion window reduction back in the congestion control topic, to ease off a network that may be under real pressure. Both reactions fire from the exact same signal.
9. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming TCP always waits for a full timeout before ever resending anything, when fast retransmission via duplicate acknowledgments is actually the faster, more common path in practice when enough data is available.","Assuming retransmission timing is a fixed, one size fits all value, rather than something TCP actively adapts per connection based on real measured conditions.","TCP infers loss, it never gets told directly that something was lost.","Timeout is the universal fallback; fast retransmission is the quicker common path.","Fast retransmission needs enough later data to trigger duplicate acknowledgments, timeout is the only catch for a lost final segment.","Sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and retransmission together form TCP complete reliability machinery."]
items: Assuming TCP always waits for a full timeout before ever resending anything, when fast retransmission via duplicate acknowledgments is actually the faster, more common path in practice when enough data is available.
Assuming retransmission timing is a fixed, one size fits all value, rather than something TCP actively adapts per connection based on real measured conditions.
TCP infers loss, it never gets told directly that something was lost.
Timeout is the universal fallback; fast retransmission is the quicker common path.
Fast retransmission needs enough later data to trigger duplicate acknowledgments, timeout is the only catch for a lost final segment.
Sequence numbers, acknowledgments, and retransmission together form TCP complete reliability machinery.
